newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Cabletron CFO blames Europe sales.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Cabletron CFO blames Europe sales.

text.p: Cabletron Systems Inc's results for the quarter ended in May suffered primarily from a decline in international sales, especially in Europe, Chief Financial Officer David Kirkpatrick said.
Late Monday, the network equipment supplier had warned it expected to post fiscal first quarter net income around $0.37 per share versus the analysts' consensus estimate of $0.50.
The earnings surprise shocked Wall Street and led analysts to slash their ratings and earnings projections. The stock spiraled down to 30-5/8, off 15-1/8 in morning trading.
In a telephone interview, Kirkpatrick attributed the expected shortfall in the quarter's financial results to a variety of factors, but primarily to international sales.
"It was really a shortfall in international and especially in Europe," the Cabletron executive said when asked to weigh the factors leading to the lower-than-expected results.
Cabletron said Monday it expected first quarter revenues of $360 to $370 million. These figures were over $30 million shy of the more than $400 million analysts had expected.
"(International) was the largest portion of the dollar shortfall of $30 million," Kirkpatrick told Reuters.
Asked if the international sales problems were related to industry-wide issues or company-specific ones, Kirkpatrick said he did not have enough data at this time to say.
He said this was the first quarter where the company had seen a significant slowdown in international sales.

In addition to international sales, Kirkpatrick said first quarter results were hurt by production problems on its newly introduced SmartSwitch products, "both in our own production and some component availablity from suppliers."

"We had some demand we weren't able to fulfill," Kirkpatrick said of the production delays. The SmartSwitch line, which began shipping in the quarter, is a key element of Cabletron's strategy to enter the low-end switch market.

Cabletron had warned that its expectations were "guarded" for the upcoming summer quarter, which is traditionally its weakest quarter due to seasonal factors. Kirkpatrick also said concerns for the quarter ended in August were tied to Europe.
"We tend to typify our summer quarter as slowest, especially for Europe, he said. "Coming off a short quarter, we are especially cautious."
Nonetheless, the company had said in its statement Monday that it remained "optimistic" about subsequent quarters.

Economic uncertainty in Europe was cited by microprocessor giant Intel Corp last week when it warned that weak European demand was expected to result in a second quarter sales decline of five to 10 percent versus the first quarter.

In early May, Cabletron's main rival, Cisco Systems Inc, had said it had encountered sluggish spending during its quarter ended in April in Germany and France, as well as Japan. Cisco executives had warned it expected France to remain "very, very sluggish" heading into the summer.
Stagnant economies, austerity measures related to European monetary union and technology transition issues are all factors, industry analysts believe.
On Monday, Cabletron also had said demand was soft for its shared media products, a mature line of business designed for computer networks that largely carry only data traffic.

Shared media is a declining portion of its business compared with newer switch products, which give computer users access to the greater network capacity necessary to download graphics or communicate via voice or video over such networks.

Network industry analyst Esmerelda Silva of International Data Corp said Cabletron has done a good job over the years of managing the transition to switch-based products from older shared media equipment.
Switch revenues accounted for about 63 percent of Cabletron's core switch and hub revenues, versus 37 percent for shared media products as of February, she estimated.

Historically, the company's core switching and hub products have produced 80 percent of its revenues, maintenance and other miscellaneous products 12 percent and systems management software about five percent.

One analyst who does not officially follow the stock but listened to the company conference call said that Cabletron's SmartSwitch products may have met with competition from Cisco's own newly introduced 5500 switches.
Cisco was the leader during 1996 in the high end switching market, with 36 percent share, followed by Cabletron with 21 percent and 11 percent for 3Com Corp, IDC estimated.

Cabletron is a small player in the low-end switch market, where it has a four percent share versus 3Com's 37 percent and Cisco's 21 percent. Cabletron's new SmartSwitch products are designed to boost its presence in the segment, Silva said.
